subject: botany
question_text: Write a brief account on gametogenesis with examples.

verification.note: Chapter 6 is sourced from the Junior Fastrack botany guide (book p.16), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star ranks and NO year citations. Only ONE source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the board-paper back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely pending. The 1+2+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book lower-cases the genus names 'pteris, cycas'; the card capitalises them. The 'diploid body needs meiosis for gametes' line is the NCERT-level simplification the book also uses — the ploidy step's why records the seed-plant nuance.

insider_note: The book lists Monera with fungi, algae and bryophytes as haploid-bodied organisms (NCERT's own grouping) — keep those examples; the examiner checks the mitosis/meiosis contrast.

steps.label: Definition
lines: The process of formation of the two
types of gametes — male and female —
steps.why: The account has to start from the word itself: gamete + genesis, the formation of the male and female gametes.
common_mistakes: Defining it as fusion of gametes — fusion is syngamy (fertilization); genesis is FORMATION.
steps.memory_tip: Genesis = formation. Gametogenesis forms the gametes; syngamy fuses them.
steps.margin_note: One boxed definition line opens the answer.

steps.label: Isogametes and heterogametes
lines: Isogametes: the two fusing gametes are
different in appearance — a male gamete
steps.why: 'With examples' points here: each gamete condition needs its name, the contrast (similar vs different), and a named organism.
common_mistakes: Writing Cladophora under heterogametes — it is the standard ISOgamete example.
Lower-casing genus names — write Cladophora, Funaria, Pteris, Cycas.
steps.memory_tip: Iso = equal (the two gametes match); hetero = different (a large still egg and a small motile male gamete).
steps.margin_note: Both terms + one example line each carries the 2 marks.

steps.label: Ploidy of gametes
lines: A haploid parent body forms gametes by
A diploid parent body needs meiosis to
steps.why: Whatever the parent's ploidy, gametes must end up haploid — a haploid body copies cells by mitosis, a diploid body must halve by meiosis somewhere in the line (in seed plants meiosis makes the spores, and the gametophyte then forms gametes by mitosis — the life-cycle answer shows this).
common_mistakes: Writing that gametes can be diploid — normal gametes are always haploid.
Saying haploid organisms use meiosis for gametes — a haploid cell cannot halve; they use mitosis.
steps.memory_tip: One rule: gametes are haploid. Haploid body → mitosis is enough; diploid body → a meiosis step is required.
steps.margin_note: The mitosis/meiosis contrast with one example set each.
